Let $N\ge0$, $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, source positions $z_j\in\mathbb C$ and charges $q_j\in\mathbb C$ for $j\in I$, and target positions equal to the same labelled positions. A root square is a closed square of side $s_0>0$ containing every source position. Its cells are the dyadic subsquares obtained by repeatedly bisecting each side. At each split use half-open child squares, with the outer top and right edges included in the last child, so every point belongs to exactly one child. A **finite quadtree** is a finite rooted tree of such cells in which each internal cell has its four geometric children and each leaf contains at most $s$ labels for a fixed integer $s\ge1$. Empty children are retained as geometric cells but are skipped in source and target lists. For a cell $C$, write $c_C$ for its center, $s_C$ for its side length, $I_C=\{j:z_j\in C\}$, and $a_C=s_C/\sqrt2$ for the radius of its circumscribed disk.

A cell pair $(C,D)$ is **source-separated from target-separated** when $R_{CD}:=|c_D-c_C|>a_C+a_D$; $C$ is the source cell and $D$ the target cell. For every such pair fix an analytic logarithm $L_{CD}$ on the open disk $\{w:|w-(c_D-c_C)|<R_{CD}\}$. This disk excludes zero and contains all differences $z_i-z_j$ with $i\in I_D$, $j\in I_C$. For each direct near particle pair $(j,i)$ fix one value $L_{ji}$ of the logarithm of $z_i-z_j$, when this difference is nonzero. Once the recursive rule below terminates, for a collision-free configuration define the exact target potential and its complex derivative using the resulting lists as follows:
Here $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ denote the far and direct near lists produced by that rule.
$$u_i:=\sum_{(j,i)\in\mathcal N}q_jL_{ji}+\sum_{\substack{(C,D)\in\mathcal F\\ i\in I_D}}\ \sum_{j\in I_C}q_jL_{CD}(z_i-z_j),\qquad g_i:=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{q_j}{z_i-z_j}.$$
Thus each ordered source-target pair contributes its source charge times the fixed direct-near branch value or the fixed far-cell branch value prescribed by its list entry. The complex derivative is independent of the chosen logarithm values.

The **recursive interaction decomposition** of an ordered pair of nonempty cells $(C,D)$ is defined as follows. If $C=D$ is a leaf, record as direct near pairs all $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. If $C=D$ is internal, replace $(C,D)$ by all ordered pairs $(E,F)$ of its nonempty children. If $C\ne D$ and $R_{CD}>a_C+a_D$, record the far cell pair $(C,D)$. If both cells are leaves and the pair is not separated, record all direct near particle pairs $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. In every other case, if exactly one cell is nonleaf, split that cell; if both are nonleaf, split the one of larger side length, breaking a tie by splitting the source cell. Replace the pair by the child pairs having nonempty source and target sets. For $N\ge1$, start at the root pair; for $N=0$, make no recursive calls and set both lists to empty. The resulting lists are the **far interaction list** $\mathcal F$ and the **direct near-pair list** $\mathcal N$. Their termination and exact pair-partition property are mathematical assertions, proved separately.

For a far pair $(C,D)$ put $\rho_{CD}=(a_C+a_D)/R_{CD}<1$ and $Q_C=\sum_{j\in I_C}|q_j|$. Two leaves are adjacent when their closed squares meet. A tree is **2:1 level-restricted** when any adjacent leaves have depths differing by at most one. It is **linear-size level-restricted for this decomposition** when it is 2:1 level-restricted and there are fixed constants $C_T,C_V$ such that its number $T$ of nonempty cells and the number $V$ of recursive cell-pair inspections satisfy $T\le C_T\max(1,N)$ and $V\le C_V\max(1,N)$. A list is **bounded** when there are fixed constants $C_F,C_N$ with $|\mathcal F|\le C_F T$ and $|\mathcal N|\le C_N\max(1,N)$. The work theorem uses these explicit counts; 2:1 balance alone is not asserted to supply them.

derivations.claim: For a cell $C$ let $h(C)$ be its remaining tree height, and for a pair $(C,D)$ use $h(C)+h(D)$. Every nonterminal call split by [F1] selects a nonleaf cell (both coordinates when $C=D$); each child call strictly lowers the height of every split coordinate and leaves any unsplit coordinate fixed. The measure is a nonnegative integer, so every branch terminates. The recursion is finitely branching (at most sixteen child pairs at a simultaneous equal-cell split), hence its finite-depth recursion tree is finite.

If the source cell is split, its child label sets are disjoint and cover the source labels, so the child Cartesian products are a disjoint cover of $I_C\times I_D$. The same statement holds when the target cell is split. When $C=D$ is internal, splitting both ordered coordinates gives all ordered child products, also disjoint. Thus each recursive replacement preserves exactly the parent pair set.

A terminal far cell pair records its entire Cartesian product $I_C\times I_D$. A terminal near pair of leaves records exactly that product with the diagonal labels removed. By step 2.1, induction from the root pair shows these terminal records cover the off-diagonal part of the root product without overlap.

A far cell pair has disjoint circumscribed disks because $R_{CD}>a_C+a_D$; hence its label sets cannot intersect and its product contains no diagonal pair. Removing the diagonal only at terminal leaf pairs therefore leaves exactly all ordered pairs $(j,i)$ with $j\ne i$, each once.

Let $\mathbb S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ with its usual surface-area measure $dS$, normalized so $\int_{\mathbb S^2}dS=4\pi$. For an integer $\ell\ge0$, let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the complex vector space of restrictions to $\mathbb S^2$ of homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials $P(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ satisfying $\Delta P=0$. Give $\mathcal H_\ell$ the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb S^2}f\overline g\,dS$, linear in the first argument. An orthonormal basis is not fixed by this definition; the addition-theorem item proves that $\dim\mathcal H_\ell=2\ell+1$ and that such a finite basis exists.

If $Y_{\ell m}\in\mathcal H_\ell$ is later chosen from an orthonormal basis and $v\ne0$, its associated homogeneous harmonic polynomial is $H_{\ell m}(v)=|v|^\ell Y_{\ell m}(v/|v|)$. At $v=0$ use the polynomial value: $H_{00}(0)=Y_{00}$ and $H_{\ell m}(0)=0$ for $\ell>0$. This is the regular-solid-harmonic convention used in the 3D evaluator.

derivations.claim: Let $\mathcal P_\ell$ be the homogeneous degree-$\ell$ polynomials in three variables; it has $\binom{\ell+2}{2}$ monomials. For a homogeneous polynomial $g$ of degree $d$, direct differentiation and Euler's identity give $\Delta(|x|^{2s}g)=2s(2d+2s+1)|x|^{2s-2}g+|x|^{2s}\Delta g$. If $\ell\ge2$, put $n=\ell-2$, $J=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, $A_j=2(j+1)(2n-2j+3)$, $c_0=1/A_0$, and $c_j=-c_{j-1}/A_j$ for $1\le j\le J$. For $f\in\mathcal P_n$, the degree-$\ell$ polynomial $q=\sum_{j=0}^Jc_j|x|^{2(j+1)}\Delta^jf$ satisfies $\Delta q=f$: the coefficients of $|x|^{2j}\Delta^jf$ telescope by $c_0A_0=1$ and $c_jA_j+c_{j-1}=0$, and $\Delta^{J+1}f=0$. Hence $\Delta:\mathcal P_\ell\to\mathcal P_{\ell-2}$ is onto; for $\ell=0,1$ the target is zero.

Restriction of a homogeneous polynomial to $\mathbb S^2$ is injective, because homogeneity recovers its value at every nonzero $x$ from its value at $x/|x|$. Rank-nullity therefore gives $\dim\mathcal H_\ell=\binom{\ell+2}{2}-\binom{\ell}{2}=2\ell+1$ for $\ell\ge2$, and direct counting gives $1$ and $3$ for $\ell=0,1$. Gram-Schmidt on any finite spanning list gives an orthonormal basis; no choice axiom is used.

For an orthonormal basis define $K_\ell(\omega,\omega')=\sum_mY_{\ell m}(\omega)\overline{Y_{\ell m}(\omega')}$. A unitary basis change leaves this sum unchanged, and rotations carry one orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_\ell$ to another, so $K_\ell$ is rotation-invariant. Thus $K_\ell(\omega,\omega)$ is constant in $\omega$; integrating it over the sphere gives $2\ell+1$, so this constant is $(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$.

Fix $\omega'$. After rotating it to the third coordinate axis, use $w=x_1+ix_2$ and $\bar w=x_1-ix_2$. A rotation sends these to $e^{i\theta}w$ and $e^{-i\theta}\bar w$, so an invariant monomial $w^a\bar w^b x_3^c$ must have $a=b$. The invariant homogeneous polynomials are therefore sums of $(x_1^2+x_2^2)^j x_3^{\ell-2j}$, whose restrictions to the sphere are polynomials $f(t)$ of degree at most $\ell$, with $t=x_3$. The polar-coordinate Laplacian is $\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$; applying it to $r^\ell f(\cos\theta)$ gives $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}f=-\ell(\ell+1)f$. For a zonal $f$, the angular term is $(\sin\theta)^{-1}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\partial_\theta f)=(1-t^2)f''-2tf'$ by $t=\cos\theta$, so $(1-t^2)f''-2tf'+\ell(\ell+1)f=0$. Writing $f(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell}a_kt^k$ yields $(k+2)(k+1)a_{k+2}+\bigl(\ell(\ell+1)-k(k+1)\bigr)a_k=0$. For $\ell\ge1$, the equation at $k=\ell-1$, using $a_{\ell+1}=0$, gives $2\ell a_{\ell-1}=0$; descending through $k=\ell-3,\ell-5,\ldots$ forces every coefficient of parity opposite to $\ell$ to vanish. For $k=\ell-2,\ell-4,\ldots$, the coefficient $\ell(\ell+1)-k(k+1)$ is positive, so each lower coefficient of parity $\ell$ is determined by the next one. Thus the zonal solution space has dimension at most one (for $\ell=0$ it is the constants). The function $K_\ell(\cdot,\omega')$ is a zonal harmonic, and $K_\ell(\omega',\omega')=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)>0$, so a nonzero such solution exists. Define $P_\ell(t)=K_\ell(\omega,\omega')/K_\ell(\omega',\omega')$ when $t=\omega\cdot\omega'$. Rotation invariance makes this depend only on $t$, and $P_\ell(1)=1$. The diagonal value in step 3.1 now gives the displayed addition theorem.

Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the finite basis sum gives $|K_\ell(\omega,\omega')|\le\sqrt{K_\ell(\omega,\omega)K_\ell(\omega',\omega')}=(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. Dividing by the diagonal constant proves $|P_\ell(t)|\le1$.

Fix $\omega'\in\mathbb S^2$ and let $u(x)=|\omega'-x|^{-1}$ for $|x|<1$. The radial formula $\Delta |x-\omega'|^{-1}=f''(r)+2f'(r)/r=0$ away from $\omega'$ shows $u$ is harmonic in the unit ball. Its homogeneous Taylor term of degree $\ell$ is therefore harmonic, since the homogeneous terms in $\Delta u=0$ of each degree vanish separately; it is also invariant under rotations fixing $\omega'$. By step 4.1 it has the form $b_\ell r^\ell P_\ell(\omega\cdot\omega')$. On the ray $x=r\omega'$, $u(r\omega')=(1-r)^{-1}=\sum_{\ell\ge0}r^\ell$, so coefficient comparison gives $b_\ell=1$. Finally $u(r\omega)=(1-2r(\omega\cdot\omega')+r^2)^{-1/2}$, whose Taylor series in $r$ has radius at least $1$: its possible denominator zeros are $t\pm i\sqrt{1-t^2}$, both of modulus one. This proves the generating identity for $0\le r<1$.

A root square is a closed square of side $s_0>0$ containing every source position. Its cells are the dyadic subsquares obtained by repeatedly bisecting each side. At each split use half-open child squares, with the outer top and right edges included in the last child, so every point belongs to exactly one child. A **finite quadtree** is a finite rooted tree of such cells in which each internal cell has its four geometric children and each leaf contains at most $s$ labels for a fixed integer $s\ge1$. Empty children are retained as geometric cells but are skipped in source and target lists. For a cell $C$, write $c_C$ for its center, $s_C$ for its side length, $I_C=\{j:z_j\in C\}$, and $a_C=s_C/\sqrt2$ for the radius of its circumscribed disk.

A cell pair $(C,D)$ is **source-separated from target-separated** when $R_{CD}:=|c_D-c_C|>a_C+a_D$; $C$ is the source cell and $D$ the target cell. For every such pair fix an analytic logarithm $L_{CD}$ on the open disk $\{w:|w-(c_D-c_C)|<R_{CD}\}$. This disk excludes zero and contains all differences $z_i-z_j$ with $i\in I_D$, $j\in I_C$. For each direct near particle pair $(j,i)$ fix one value $L_{ji}$ of the logarithm of $z_i-z_j$, when this difference is nonzero. Once the recursive rule below terminates, for a collision-free configuration define the exact target potential and its complex derivative using the resulting lists as follows:
Here $\mathcal F$ and $\mathcal N$ denote the far and direct near lists produced by that rule.
$$u_i:=\sum_{(j,i)\in\mathcal N}q_jL_{ji}+\sum_{\substack{(C,D)\in\mathcal F\\ i\in I_D}}\ \sum_{j\in I_C}q_jL_{CD}(z_i-z_j),\qquad g_i:=\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{q_j}{z_i-z_j}.$$
Thus each ordered source-target pair contributes its source charge times the fixed direct-near branch value or the fixed far-cell branch value prescribed by its list entry. The complex derivative is independent of the chosen logarithm values.

The **recursive interaction decomposition** of an ordered pair of nonempty cells $(C,D)$ is defined as follows. If $C=D$ is a leaf, record as direct near pairs all $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. If $C=D$ is internal, replace $(C,D)$ by all ordered pairs $(E,F)$ of its nonempty children. If $C\ne D$ and $R_{CD}>a_C+a_D$, record the far cell pair $(C,D)$. If both cells are leaves and the pair is not separated, record all direct near particle pairs $(j,i)\in I_C\times I_D$ with $j\ne i$. In every other case, if exactly one cell is nonleaf, split that cell; if both are nonleaf, split the one of larger side length, breaking a tie by splitting the source cell. Replace the pair by the child pairs having nonempty source and target sets. For $N\ge1$, start at the root pair; for $N=0$, make no recursive calls and set both lists to empty. The resulting lists are the **far interaction list** $\mathcal F$ and the **direct near-pair list** $\mathcal N$. Their termination and exact pair-partition property are mathematical assertions, proved separately.

For a far pair $(C,D)$ put $\rho_{CD}=(a_C+a_D)/R_{CD}<1$ and $Q_C=\sum_{j\in I_C}|q_j|$. Two leaves are adjacent when their closed squares meet. A tree is **2:1 level-restricted** when any adjacent leaves have depths differing by at most one. It is **linear-size level-restricted for this decomposition** when it is 2:1 level-restricted and there are fixed constants $C_T,C_V$ such that its number $T$ of nonempty cells and the number $V$ of recursive cell-pair inspections satisfy $T\le C_T\max(1,N)$ and $V\le C_V\max(1,N)$. A list is **bounded** when there are fixed constants $C_F,C_N$ with $|\mathcal F|\le C_F T$ and $|\mathcal N|\le C_N\max(1,N)$. Use the data, quadtree and interaction decomposition of [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]]. Fix an expansion order $p\ge1$. If two different labels have the same position, return status `collision` before evaluating any singular interaction: the requested potential is undefined. The tree and point-to-cell membership are preprocessing inputs; their construction is not part of the arithmetic passes below.

Using the supplied membership data, make a root-first list of nonempty cells: at each nonempty internal cell inspect its four children and recurse only into children $E$ with $I_E\ne\varnothing$; never descend into an empty subtree. Use the reverse list order for the bottom-up pass and the root-first order for the top-down pass. Use exact complex arithmetic throughout. For each nonempty leaf $C$ form the particle-to-multipole (P2M) moments
$$M_n(C)=\sum_{j\in I_C}q_j(z_j-c_C)^n,\qquad 0\le n\le p.$$

$$M_n(C)=\sum_{\substack{E\text{ child of }C\\ I_E\ne\varnothing}}\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(c_E-c_C)^{n-r}M_r(E).$$

$$L_k(D)\mathrel{+}=(-1)^{k+1}\left(\frac{M_0(C)}{k\delta^k}+\sum_{n=1}^p\binom{n+k-1}{k}\frac{M_n(C)}{n\delta^{n+k}}\right),\quad 1\le k\le p.$$

$$L_j(E)\mathrel{+}=\sum_{k=j}^p\binom kj L_k(D)(c_E-c_D)^{k-j},\qquad 0\le j\le p.$$
